stem: Seven-year-old Lotta has had vomiting, anorexia, low-grade fever, and right lower quadrant abdominal pain that began periumbilically. You think she has acute appendicitis. Which one of the following would you expect to find on abdominal examination?

options.text: Abdominal pain in the right lower quadrant, aggravated by movement and flushed face
Reduced skin turgor, abdominal pain in the central region and both lower quadrants, tummy soft
Negative Psoas sign, right and left inguinal fossa pain, no guarding
No McBurney tenderness, Rowsing’s sign negative

explanation: Acute appendicitis typically causes initial periumbilical pain that localises to the right lower quadrant, with pain worsened by movement and local tenderness/guarding on examination.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Emergency Medicine - Abdominal pain

rationale: The vignette describes classic appendicitis progression from periumbilical pain to right lower quadrant pain with systemic features. The option that most closely reflects expected abdominal examination findings is A.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: this best matches appendicitis with right lower quadrant tenderness and movement-related pain.
optionExplanations.B: Suggests dehydration/other abdominal pain; a soft abdomen is less typical of established appendicitis.
optionExplanations.C: Negative psoas sign and bilateral inguinal pain are not typical features of appendicitis.
optionExplanations.D: Appendicitis often causes McBurney tenderness and may have a positive Rovsing sign, so this is contrary to expectation.
optionExplanations.E: Periumbilical pain can occur early in appendicitis, but a soft abdomen without localisation is less typical for the expected examination finding here.
